title: Constants and Readonly Values
learningObjectives: Declare a const local or member and explain why its value cannot be reassigned.
Declare a readonly field and initialize it at declaration or in a constructor.
Distinguish compile-time constants from runtime-initialized values.
Choose const or readonly according to when a value becomes known.
Explain why readonly does not necessarily make a referenced object immutable.

understand.concept: A constant represents a value that must not change. C# provides const for compile-time constants and readonly for fields that can be assigned only at declaration or in an appropriate constructor. They both prevent ordinary later reassignment but have different initialization and compilation rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Stable values such as unit conversions and object-specific settings should not be accidentally changed. Choosing the correct feature also avoids versioning surprises when libraries expose constants.
understand.analogy: const is like a rule printed permanently before a form is distributed. readonly is like a sealed label whose value is set when the object or type is initialized.
understand.analogyLimit: readonly restricts assignment to the field, not necessarily mutation of an object referenced by that field. A readonly field can refer to a mutable object.

explain.narrative:
## const

A const field or local must be initialized with a compile-time constant expression. A class const member is implicitly static and cannot be assigned later. Numeric literals and expressions made from constants are common uses.

## readonly

A readonly field can be initialized where it is declared or assigned in the relevant constructor. A static readonly field is assigned at declaration or in a static constructor; an instance readonly field can also be assigned in an instance constructor. Its value may be determined at runtime.

## Choosing between them

Use const for values genuinely fixed at compile time. Use readonly when initialization depends on runtime information or when a library value may change between versions without consumers needing recompilation.

## Important distinction

readonly protects the field assignment, not the full object graph behind a reference. The examples use immutable values to keep the behaviour clear.

## Version baseline

const and readonly are long-standing C# features supported by .NET 10 and C# 14.
